title: Time Has Its Turns, and Death Its Causes
intro: One of Abu al-Atahiya's poems of renunciation (zuhd); the sources do not say when or why he wrote it. It opens with a run of short maxims on the turns of fortune, the many causes of death and the hope that never leaves a man, then rebukes the one who sells his faith for the world and plays while death rushes at him, warns against trusting wishes, and urges fairness and kindness. It ends with a friend closing his companion's eyes and covering him, weeping a little, burying him and forgetting him, and with the thought that everyone will reach his appointed time and meet his deeds. Louis Cheikho's edition of the diwan, al-Anwar al-Zahiya, heads it as a poem on the deceit of vain hopes and calls it “among the finest of his poetry”. Ibn Abd al-Barr quotes two of its half-lines under Abu al-Atahiya's name, and the modern critic Shawqi Dayf quotes five of its lines as an example of his songs of death and passing.

translation: Time has its turns, and death its causes;
man has his hopes, and people are all alike.
1.sharh: Fortune passes from one people to another, death has many ways in, and still no one stops hoping; in this everyone is the same. The line is four short balanced clauses, each a maxim.

translation: And lessons never cease, each with matter to ponder;
a decree runs through them, and God set it running.
2.sharh: Time keeps bringing lessons, each with something to reflect on. They do not happen by chance: a decree drives them, and God set it in motion, which is the greatest lesson of all.

translation: A man of shifting soul weeps and laughs;
God makes him laugh, and God makes him weep.
3.sharh: A man's moods are not his own: he weeps and laughs as God turns him, as in the Quran's “it is He who makes laugh and makes weep” (53:43). The second half reverses the order of the first.

translation: The man in trouble is the one whose side is shunned;
people are wherever wealth and standing are.
4.sharh: Whoever falls into misfortune, poverty or illness, is left alone, since no one expects anything from him; people gather where money and rank are. Their friendship follows their interest, not loyalty.

translation: All creatures are my Lord's creation, and He directs them;
each is a slave, and God is his master.
5.sharh: Every creature is God's making and under His direction: each is a slave who owns nothing of his affairs, and God owns him. So, the next line says, a slave does well only by returning to his master.

translation: Blessed is the slave who turns back to his master;
the slave whose heart turns back, who sighs in prayer, has won.
6.sharh: Happy is whoever returns to God in repentance; the true winner is the one whose heart turns to Him and who calls on Him humbly. Since all creatures are slaves, their happiness lies in going back to their master.

translation: You who sell your faith for this world and its vanities,
you accept for your faith a thing not worth it.
7.sharh: He addresses the man who gives up his religion for worldly gain and marvels at the bargain: what he got is worth less than what he gave, like a seller who has been cheated.

translation: How long will you go on in idle play and games,
while death swoops towards you, its mouth gaping?
8.sharh: He rebukes the heedless man for taking so long to wake: he plays while death rushes at him, open-mouthed, to swallow him. The question wants no answer; modern books on rhetoric cite it as one that expresses impatience.

translation: Not everything a man wishes for does he attain;
many a man's death lies in what he wished for.
9.sharh: A man does not get all he wishes for, and that may be as well, since what he longs for may kill him. Al-Mutanabbi, more than a century later, opens a famous line with these very words.

translation: Wishes are a delusion, a straying and a whim;
perhaps a man's death lies in the very thing he loves.
10.sharh: Wishes deceive: they lead a man away from what is right and after what his soul desires. The second half repeats the last line in other words: a man may perish through the very thing he wants.

translation: You are fooled, out of ignorance, by the world and its glitter;
the wretched one is he whom his world deceives.
11.sharh: Only ignorance makes a man trust the world's finery, and real wretchedness is not poverty or hardship but being fooled by this world and so kept from the next.

translation: It is as if a living man, long as his health has lasted,
were already in the throes of death, which cover him.
12.sharh: However long a man has stayed well, he may as well be dying already: what is coming is near, and long health does not put it off. The line brings the distant end into the present.

translation: People are asleep to what is meant for them,
and events keep shaking them and waking them.
13.sharh: People live as if asleep, heedless of what God has decreed for them, while misfortunes keep coming to shake them awake, and still they sleep. Heedlessness is a sleep, and calamities are the call to rise.

translation: Many a day its good news came in,
then its good news changed at the voice announcing a death.
14.sharh: A day can begin with happy news and end with news of a death, turning celebration into mourning. The same words, “its good news”, are in both halves: first arriving, then turned into the announcement of a death.

translation: Be fair, may you be guided, if you want your due:
do not want for people what you would not want yourself.
15.sharh: Whoever wants his own due should give others theirs, and wish on no one what he would not accept. This is the sense of the hadith “none of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself”.

translation: Do not belittle the least act of kindness;
do good, for the outcome of doing good is the best.
16.sharh: No good deed is too small to do; do what good you can, since kindness returns to the doer only as good. The first half echoes the hadith “do not belittle any kindness, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face”.

translation: Every matter must have an end;
and the best of your affairs is the one whose end you praise.
17.sharh: Every deed comes to an end, so it is judged by how it ends, and the best is the one whose ending a man is glad of. The outcome of kindness, in the last line, is such an ending.

translation: We play, while our evenings and our mornings belong to death;
whom death's face does not meet at morning, it meets at evening.
18.sharh: We play without a care, though death owns every hour: if it does not come for a man in the morning, it comes in the evening. Death is given a face, appearing at the door like a visitor.

translation: How many a young man's journey to death has drawn near;
and a young man's best provision for death is fear of God.
19.sharh: Death does not wait for old age; many young men are nearer to it than they know. Death is a journey, and its best provision is piety, as in the Quran's “take provision, and the best provision is piety” (2:197).

translation: How near death is in this world, and how terrible;
how bitter the fruit of this world, and how sweet.
20.sharh: He marvels that death is so close and so dreadful, and that what the world gives is both sweet and bitter: sweet while enjoyed, bitter in what follows. The second half puts both opposites in the one fruit.

translation: How often a man has striven and schemed against people
for something, then passed on and left it behind.
21.sharh: A man competes and plots to win some worldly thing before others, then dies and leaves it behind, taking nothing; all the rivalry is over what will be left. In the Arabic a word runs across the break.

translation: While a tender friend delights in the companion he loves,
suddenly one day he is closing his eyes and covering him.
22.sharh: Amid a friendship's happiness death comes without warning: one day the friend finds himself closing his companion's eyes and drawing a cloth over him. The Arabic pairs bayna, “while”, with idh, “when suddenly”, to carry the surprise.

translation: He weeps over him a little, then carries him out,
gives the earth hold of him, then forgets him.
23.sharh: The friend's grief is short: he weeps a little, carries the body out to the grave, hands it to the earth and forgets it. The repeated “then” shrinks the distance between mourning and forgetting.

translation: Everyone with a set term will one day reach it,
and everyone who has done deeds will one day meet them.
24.sharh: Every living being will surely reach its appointed time, and everyone will meet his deeds, good or bad, on the day of reckoning. The poem closes on two parallel halves: death, and what comes after it.

1.1.3.head: دُوَل
1.1.3.meaning: Duwal: turns of fortune, a turn at wealth or victory that goes to one side and then the other.

1.1.6.head: عِلَل
1.1.6.meaning: Illnesses; the word also means causes.

2.1.3.head: عِبَر
2.1.3.meaning: Lessons, warnings: what a man learns from what has happened before.

4.2.5.head: الجاه
4.2.5.meaning: Jah: standing, rank, especially in the eyes of those in power.

6.1.1.meaning: Tuba: a word of blessing, “joy to him”, from the root of “good”; it is also said to be the name of a tree in Paradise.

6.2.6.meaning: Awwah: one who sighs in fear and humility before God, or who prays much. The Quran calls Abraham awwah (11:75).

7.2.5.head: يَسوى
7.2.5.meaning: Is worth it. The usual form is yusawi; the lexicographers call yaswa rare, perhaps a Hijazi usage.

8.2.4-5.head: فَغَرَ فاه
8.2.4-5.meaning: “Gaping its mouth”: open-mouthed, ready to swallow.

12.2.4-5.head: سَكرَة المَوت
12.2.4-5.meaning: “The drunkenness of death”: the throes of dying, which overcome a man as drink does.

14.2.4.head: النَّعي
14.2.4.meaning: Na'y: the announcement of a death, the news that someone has died.

15.1.2.head: هَدى
15.1.2.meaning: “May you be guided”: a blessing set in the middle of the command.

18.1.1.head: لَها
18.1.1.meaning: We play. Shukri Faisal's edition and al-Anwar al-Zahiya have talhu, “you play”; Shawqi Dayf quotes the line with nalhu, as the reciter says it.

18.1.3-4.head: مُمسى وَمُصبَح
18.1.3-4.meaning: “Our evening and our morning”: our coming to evening and to morning, so every hour of our days.

21.1.7.meaning: Fi-: the start of fihi, “in it”, which ends at the start of the second half. Arabic prosody lets a word run across the break.

22.2.5.head: سَجّى
22.2.5.meaning: Covered him: drew a cloth over the dead body.

23.2.1-3.head: أَمكَنَ الأَرضَ مِنه
23.2.1-3.meaning: “Gives the earth hold of him”: buries him.
